papers.title: The Gp78 ubiquitin E3 ligase drives mitophagy by regulating omegasome formation
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the Gp78 ubiquitin E3 ligase, located on the endoplasmic reticulum, controls mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria are selectively degraded. The researchers show that Gp78 regulates the formation of omegasomes, specialized ER-derived structures that serve as platforms for autophagosome biogenesis around damaged mitochondria. This links ER-mitochondria contact sites and ubiquitin signaling to the initiation of autophagic membrane formation during mitophagy.
papers.why: Understanding molecular regulators of mitophagy such as Gp78 and omegasome formation is directly relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy mechanisms in neurons, which could inform interpretation of spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic signatures of autophagic dysfunction in specific neuronal populations.

papers.title: Spatial multiomics in biomedical research: advances beyond transcriptomics.
papers.summary: This paper reviews recent progress in spatial multiomics, a field that combines multiple molecular data types—like transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics—while preserving their spatial context within tissue. It highlights technological advances that go beyond spatial transcriptomics alone, showing how integrating multiple omics layers can reveal richer biological insight into tissue architecture and cell states. The review likely discusses methodological challenges, emerging platforms, and applications across various biomedical research areas.
papers.why: Since your PhD work integrates spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics to study mitophagy and autophagy in neurons and perineuronal nets, this review could offer valuable methodological context and highlight emerging multiomic approaches applicable to your research design.

papers.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
papers.summary: This paper appears to describe a newly revealed mechanism by which autophagy-related machinery contributes to the formation or release of extracellular vesicles (EVs). Autophagic EVs may represent a distinct subtype of vesicles that carry cargo processed through autophagy pathways rather than conventional exosome routes. The abstract text provided is minimal, so specific molecular players and experimental systems are not detailed here.
papers.why: Understanding how autophagy machinery intersects with extracellular vesicle biogenesis could reveal new routes by which neurons dispose of or communicate mitophagy/autophagy cargo into the extracellular space, potentially affecting perineuronal net composition or local signaling detectable by spatial omics.

papers.title: A Human Neuronal Cell Model of Endogenous TDP-43 A315T Reveals Altered Protein Dynamics and Disease-Relevant Cellular Dysfunction
papers.summary: This study creates a human neuronal cell model carrying an endogenous TDP-43 A315T mutation, a genetic variant linked to ALS and frontotemporal dementia. The researchers use this model to examine how the mutation changes TDP-43 protein behavior, such as its localization and stability within cells. They connect these molecular changes to broader cellular dysfunctions relevant to neurodegenerative disease.
papers.why: TDP-43 pathology involves disrupted protein clearance mechanisms that intersect with autophagy and mitophagy pathways, offering mechanistic insight relevant to neuronal proteostasis studied in this PhD project.

papers.title: Mitochondrial resilience: a convergent framework for pathogenesis and neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: This paper proposes 'mitochondrial resilience' as a unifying concept for understanding how neurons cope with or succumb to mitochondrial stress in Parkinson's disease. It frames disease pathogenesis and potential neuroprotective strategies around the balance between mitochondrial damage and the cell's capacity to buffer, repair, or clear damaged mitochondria. The abstract suggests this framework could reconcile diverse findings across genetic and cellular models of Parkinson's disease into a coherent picture of mitochondrial quality control failure.
papers.why: Since mitophagy is central to your PhD work on neuronal mitochondrial quality control, this paper's conceptual framework on mitochondrial resilience and mitophagy failure in Parkinson's disease could sharpen the mechanistic lens you apply to interneuron vulnerability and dysfunction.

papers.title: Glutaminase contributes to MYC-induced cell-autonomous autophagy and to Ras  <sup>V12</sup>  -dependent non-autonomous autophagy in the Drosophila wing disc epithelium
papers.summary: This study examines how the enzyme glutaminase contributes to autophagy driven by two different oncogenic signals, MYC and Ras^V12, in the Drosophila wing disc epithelium. It distinguishes cell-autonomous autophagy (triggered by MYC within the same cells) from non-cell-autonomous autophagy (triggered by Ras^V12 in neighboring cells). The findings link metabolic enzyme activity to autophagy regulation and cell-to-cell signaling in an epithelial tissue model.
papers.why: Although this work is in a fly epithelial model rather than neurons, its mechanistic insights into metabolic regulation of autophagy and non-autonomous signaling between cells could inform interpretation of spatial metabolomics data on mitophagy/autophagy pathways in brain tissue.

papers.title: Characterizing the molecular mechanisms underlying aluminium-induced disruptions in neuronal survival pathways.
papers.summary: This study investigates how aluminium exposure disrupts molecular pathways that neurons rely on to survive. It likely examines stress responses, protein aggregation, or organelle dysfunction triggered by aluminium toxicity in brain cells. The work aims to clarify mechanistic links between environmental metal exposure and neuronal degeneration.
papers.why: Aluminium-induced disruption of neuronal survival pathways may implicate mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction as a shared mechanism relevant to this project's focus on neuronal quality control processes.
